name: Incident Runbooks
subtitle: Ordered checklists: stabilise, diagnose, fix, document

cmds.desc: 1. Status, latency and which resolver answered
2. Same query against a public resolver: slow too = path or ISP; fast = your resolver
3. Works over TCP but not UDP = fragmentation, MTU or UDP/53 filtering
4. Works with checking disabled but SERVFAIL otherwise = DNSSEC validation problem
5. Is the resolver listening, and which process?

cmds.cmd: journalctl -u named -u unbound -u systemd-resolved --since "15 min ago" | tail -50
cmds.desc: 6. Resolver logs for timeouts and upstream errors

cmds.cmd: for ns in $(dig +short NS example.com); do echo $ns; dig +short +time=2 +tries=1 @$ns example.com; done
cmds.desc: 7. Test each authoritative server: one dead server causes intermittent failures
8. A full conntrack table drops UDP queries
9. Interface errors and drops
10. Outbound rate: a saturated uplink drops DNS replies. If it is far above normal, find the sender with ss -tunap and tcpdump top talkers
1. Confirm the symptom and the status code
2. Which backend servers does the load balancer consider UP or DOWN?
3. Termination flags: sH = backend headers timeout, SC = connect failed, cD = client timeout
4. Is the application running and recently restarted?
5. Does the backend answer its health check locally?
6. Recv-Q on the app listener: a full accept queue refuses connections
7. Accept-queue overflows since boot

cmds.cmd: echo "set server be_app/web1 state drain" | socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
cmds.desc: 8. Drain the bad node so users stop hitting it
9. Kubernetes: roll back to the last working revision
10. Wait until the rollout is healthy again
1. Which filesystem is full?
2. Inodes full instead? (free space but cannot create files)
3. Find the biggest directory, then repeat one level down
4. Deleted files still open: restart the holding process to release space
5. Shrink the journal
6. Container images, layers and volumes
7. Single large files
8. Files hidden underneath a mount point (umount /mnt/rootview afterwards)
9. Truncate a runaway log in place, then fix the logging/rotation
1. Is the port reachable at all? Refused = nothing listening; timeout = firewall or network
2. Client debug: where does it stop (connect, key exchange, auth)?
3. On the console: is sshd running?
4. A config error prevents sshd from starting
5. Is it listening on the expected address?
6. Server log of the failed attempt
7. Firewall rules
8. Is your address banned?
9. A full root filesystem breaks logins
10. Permissions: home must not be group/world-writable, .ssh 700, keys 600
11. Client side: remove a stale host key after a reinstall
1. Load trend: rising, steady or falling?
2. CPU-bound (r high), I/O-bound (b high, wa high) or swapping (si/so)?
3. Tasks stuck in uninterruptible sleep point at storage or NFS
4. Disk latency and utilisation
5. Available memory
6. Kernel-reported problems
7. Top processes
8. Which service is responsible?
9. Pressure stall info: which resource are tasks waiting on?
1. State and last log lines
2. Full error with context
3. The unit as systemd sees it, including overrides
4. Unit file mistakes
5. Is the port already taken?
6. Permissions along a whole path
7. SELinux denial?
8. Related errors since boot

cmds.cmd: systemctl reset-failed SERVICE && systemctl start SERVICE
cmds.desc: 9. Clear start-rate limiting and try again
1. Baseline: which node holds the virtual IP?

cmds.cmd: while true; do date +%T; curl -s -m 1 -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://192.0.2.100/; sleep 0.5; done
cmds.desc: 2. Terminal 1: continuous probe to measure the outage window
3. Terminal 2: watch VRRP advertisements
4. On the MASTER: trigger the failover
5. On the BACKUP: did it take the VIP? How many probes failed?
6. From a client: does the MAC address change (switch has learned the move)?
7. Restore the original node
8. Check preempt behaviour and whether it flapped back
1. Measure outbound rate and compare with normal
2. Connections with owning process

cmds.cmd: tcpdump -nni eth0 -c 2000 udp | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
cmds.desc: 3. Top destinations: one peer with thousands of packets = flood
4. What is the sender? Deleted binary or odd path, and which container?
5. Preserve evidence before you remove anything
6. Contain: block egress to the destination (or scale the workload to zero)
7. Contain a compromised pod and stop GitOps from restoring it (change replicas in Git too)
8. Check for UPnP port mappings that exposed the service
9. Hunt for other deleted-binary processes
10. Executables dropped recently; also check config/plugin directories on persistent volumes

cmds.cmd: echo | openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject -issuer
cmds.desc: 1. What certificate is actually served, and when does it expire?
2. Is the chain complete (leaf, intermediate)?
3. Is the local clock correct?
4. Is the renewal working, and which cert does the service read?
5. Test renewal
6. Why did the last renewal fail?
7. Reload the service so it picks up the new certificate
8. cert-manager: events and conditions
1. Everything that is not healthy
2. Events: image pull, scheduling, probes, OOM
3. Logs of the crashed container
4. Recent cluster events

cmds.cmd: kubectl top nodes && kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory | head
cmds.desc: 5. Resource pressure

cmds.cmd: kubectl describe node NODE | grep -A8 Conditions
cmds.desc: 6. Node conditions: MemoryPressure, DiskPressure
7. Unbound volume claims keep pods Pending
8. Roll back a bad release
9. Last termination reason and exit code (137 = OOMKilled)
1. What is pending?
2. Simulate: any removals or kernel changes?
3. Out-of-tree modules will rebuild for the new kernel?
4. Move workloads off (or drain the server from the load balancer)
5. Apply updates
6. Reboot
7. New kernel running and no failed units?
8. Return the node to service
9. Any services still on old libraries?
Load average counts runnable tasks plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (state D)
Free is untouched memory; available estimates what applications can get, including reclaimable cache
State D: uninterruptible sleep, usually blocked on I/O; cannot be killed until the I/O returns
A zombie is already dead: fix or restart the parent
Exit code 137 is 128+9: killed by SIGKILL, typically the OOM killer
initramfs: small temporary root filesystem with the drivers needed to find and mount the real root
After is ordering only; Wants pulls the other unit in
Disk full but du disagrees: inodes exhausted, deleted files held open (lsof +L1), or a mount hiding files
XFS can grow but never shrink
SYN flood defence: SYN cookies, rate limiting, upstream filtering
Small requests work but big ones hang: MTU or path MTU discovery with blocked ICMP; clamp the MSS
DNS failure types: SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN and a timeout
Forgetting to bump the SOA serial means secondaries do not pick up the change
Before a planned DNS change, lower the TTL at least one old TTL ahead
Missing intermediate certificate: works on some clients, fails on others
TLS termination decrypts at the load balancer so it can inspect and route; passthrough forwards encrypted bytes untouched
Patch a kernel at scale in rings: test, canary, rolling waves, drain from the load balancer, health checks, rollback plan
Idempotent: running it again changes nothing once the desired state is reached
